full_title: BUREAU OF CUSTOMS EMPLOYEES ASSOCIATION (BOCEA), REPRESENTED BY ITS NATIONAL PRESIDENT MR. ROMULO A. PAGULAYAN, PETITIONER, VS. HON. ROZZANO RUFINO B. BIAZON (IN HIS CAPACITY AS COMMISSIONER, BUREAU OF CUSTOMS), HON. CESAR V. PURISIMA (IN HIS CAPACITY AS SECRETARY OF FINANCE), HON. MAR A. ROXAS (IN HIS CAPACITY AS FORMER SECRETARY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION AND COMMUNICATIONS), HON. JOSEPH EMILIO A. ABAYA (IN HIS CAPACITY AS INCUMBENT SECRETARY OF THE DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION AND COMMUNICATIONS), RESPONDENTS.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: X. Administrative Law > C. Powers of Administrative Agencies > 1. Quasi-legislative or Rulemaking Power > b. Requisites for Validity
topics: Expanded certiorari jurisdiction over quasi-legislative acts
Hierarchy of courts and exhaustion of administrative remedies in expanded certiorari
Ordinance-making power of the Executive (shifting schedules)
Administrative issuances cannot contravene the statute (Sec. 3506, TCCP)
Overtime pay of Customs personnel under Sec. 1508, RA 10863 (CMTA)

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics

other_subjects.syllabus_topic: I. General Principles > G. Hierarchy of Courts

doctrine:
**A petition for certiorari and prohibition under the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction (Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 1, par. 2) is a proper remedy to question quasi-legislative acts** of executive officials, such as administrative orders, memoranda, and circulars. It remains subject to the **hierarchy of courts** (the petition must be filed with the lowest court of concurrent jurisdiction, here the CA, unless the higher court grants an exemption) and to **exhaustion of administrative remedies**, which applies whether the assailed act is quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, or purely regulatory, and which is how ripeness shows itself in the case of administrative acts (reiterating *Association of Medical Clinics for Overseas Workers v. GCC Approved Medical Centers Association*). The Court may relax these rules, as it did here, because the overtime pay of Customs employees had long been debated and repeatedly litigated.

On the merits: (1) requiring Customs personnel to work three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service, to limit overtime, is a **valid exercise of the Executive's ordinance-making power**, which is inherent in executive control (not delegated by Congress) and may be delegated to subordinate executive officials. (2) **An administrative issuance that goes beyond or contradicts the statute it implements is invalid and is issued with grave abuse of discretion.** Before RA No. 10863, Section 3506 of the Tariff and Customs Code required overtime to be paid by "importers, shippers or other persons served" (including airlines, per *Carbonilla v. Board of Airline Representatives*). Memoranda shifting the cost to the national government at government rates were therefore invalid. (3) Section 1508 of RA No. 10863 (CMTA), effective June 16, 2016, adopted that same policy, so the memoranda were invalid only from August 1, 2012 to June 16, 2016.
facts:
The Bureau of Customs Employees Association (BOCEA) challenged four issuances. (1) Customs Administrative Order No. 7-2011 (July 15, 2011) prescribed official work hours at NAIA and other international airports, set three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service, and stated the policy on night-shift differential. (2) A Memorandum of Finance Secretary Purisima (August 3, 2012) directed that the 24/7 shifting also be implemented at seaports and other areas to avoid charging overtime pay. It required a customs order expressly prohibiting BOC personnel from charging overtime pay against private entities, since overtime would be paid by the national government at government rates, and it barred personnel from accepting any payment, meals, or transportation from private entities for overtime. (3) A Memorandum of Commissioner Biazon (August 10, 2012) stated that the BOC, applying government rates, would pay all overtime work and would stop charging private entities for overtime effective August 1, 2012. (4) Customs Memorandum Circular No. 195-2012 (August 28, 2012) explained that the shifting schedule was meant to avoid overtime work, in response to airline complaints.

The issuances followed a July 31, 2012 Memorandum from the Finance Secretary to the President. After consultation with airlines and various agencies, it reported that payment of government personnel's overtime by airlines and other private entities was "a deterrent to the tourism industry" and an "irregular activity." The issuances were then made upon the President's instructions. They ended the long practice of Customs employees charging overtime pay against private airlines and other entities served.

On March 7, 2013, BOCEA filed directly with the Supreme Court a petition for certiorari, prohibition, and injunction. It claimed that the issuances violated Article VI, Sections 1 and 29(1) of the Constitution, Section 3506 of the Tariff and Customs Code (TCCP), and labor laws, and were issued with grave abuse of discretion and without due process. The OSG countered that the petition was procedurally infirm and that the issuances were valid exercises of administrative authority over BOC personnel.
issues: Whether direct recourse to the Supreme Court through a petition for certiorari, prohibition, and injunction is proper.

Whether respondents committed grave abuse of discretion in issuing the assailed orders and memoranda adopting a 24/7 shifting policy and charging overtime of Customs employees only against the government and not against private entities.
ruling:
**1. Certiorari was available, but the petition disregarded the hierarchy of courts and exhaustion of administrative remedies; the Court nonetheless resolved it on the merits.** Under the second paragraph of Article VIII, Section 1, judicial power includes the duty to determine grave abuse of discretion by "any branch or instrumentality of the Government" (*Francisco v. House of Representatives*). This expanded jurisdiction differs from traditional certiorari as a supervisory writ over inferior courts and quasi-judicial bodies. **Thus, although respondents exercised quasi-legislative powers, a petition for certiorari, prohibition, and injunction was the appropriate remedy under the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction.** But even then, the petition must be filed with the lowest court of concurrent jurisdiction, the CA, unless the higher court grants an exemption (*Association of Medical Clinics*; *Rosales v. ERC*; *Kalipunan ng Damayang Mahihirap v. Robredo*). The Supreme Court "is a court of last resort, not a court of first instance." Petitioners also had to exhaust administrative remedies first, a requirement that applies to quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, and regulatory acts alike and that goes into ripeness. The proper route was: reconsideration or review by the Commissioner of Customs, appeal to the Secretary of Finance, then the Office of the President, then the CA under Rule 43, and finally the Supreme Court under Rule 45. Still, because the overtime pay of Customs employees "has been the subject of long debate and repeated litigation," the Court set aside procedural rules and decided the merits.

**2. The petition was partly meritorious.**

- **The shifting schedule is valid.** Requiring three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service and limiting overtime to weekends and holidays was a valid and reasonable exercise of the Executive's ordinance-making power. Citing *Province of Pampanga v. Romulo*, that power "is not a delegated authority from the legislature, but is a consequence of executive control over officials of the executive branch," and the President may delegate it to subordinate officials. CAO No. 7-2011 is valid.
- **Exempting private entities from paying overtime was invalid when issued.** Section 3506 of the TCCP allowed Customs employees to be assigned to overtime work "when the service rendered is to be paid for by importers, shippers or other persons served," at rates not less than those paid to employees of private enterprise. *Carbonilla* upheld that provision as complete and held that airline companies, not all taxpayers through national funds, are liable for such overtime. **By exempting airlines and private entities and making the national government pay at government rates, respondents went beyond the law and contravened *Carbonilla*.**
- **RA No. 10863 later adopted the same policy.** RA No. 10863 (Customs Modernization and Tariff Act), approved May 30, 2016 and effective June 16, 2016, repealed Section 3506. Its Section 1508 provides that overtime is paid "by the Bureau, according to service fees fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance." It also drops the floor tied to private-enterprise rates and allows additional service fees when applicable. This policy shift was within Congress's discretion and is not subject to judicial review. It legalized respondents' policy from June 16, 2016. **Respondents therefore committed grave abuse of discretion only in prohibiting the collection of overtime from private entities before June 16, 2016.**
- **Monetary prejudice is for the trial courts.** The national government was prejudiced to the extent of the overtime it paid during that four-year period. Customs employees were prejudiced only by the difference, if any, between private-enterprise overtime rates and the rates actually paid. These are evidentiary matters for the trial courts, because the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts.
disposition: The petition was PARTIALLY GRANTED. CAO No. 7-2011 (July 15, 2011), prescribing official work hours at NAIA and other international airports, a shifting schedule of three 8-hour shifts for continuous 24-hour service, and the night-shift differential policy, was DECLARED VALID until superseded. For the period from their effectivity on August 1, 2012 until the effectivity of RA No. 10863 on June 16, 2016, the following were DECLARED INVALID: the Finance Secretary's Memorandum dated August 3, 2012; the Customs Commissioner's Memorandum dated August 10, 2012; and CMC No. 195-2012 dated August 28, 2012. Before June 16, 2016, overtime work of BOC personnel should continue to be paid by importers, shippers, or other entities served, including private airlines, under the laws and jurisprudence then in force. Any resulting monetary prejudice to the government or to petitioners must be raised in the proper administrative or judicial proceeding.

bar_questions.q: In September 2013, the Secretary of Finance and the Commissioner of Customs issued memoranda that (1) required all Customs personnel at international airports to work in three 8-hour shifts to provide continuous 24-hour service and to limit overtime work, and (2) prohibited Customs personnel from charging overtime pay to airline companies, providing instead that all overtime would be paid by the national government at government rates. At the time, Section 3506 of the Tariff and Customs Code provided that Customs employees may be assigned to overtime work "when the service rendered is to be paid for by importers, shippers or other persons served," at rates not lower than those paid by private enterprise. The Customs employees' union challenges both directives. Rule on the validity of each.

alac.answer: The shifting-schedule directive is valid, but the directive prohibiting the charging of overtime to airlines is invalid for having been issued with grave abuse of discretion.
alac.legal_basis: The Executive's ordinance-making power is not delegated by the legislature but is a consequence of executive control over officials of the executive branch; the President may adopt rules and delegate this power to subordinate executive officials (Province of Pampanga v. Romulo). Administrative issuances, however, cannot go beyond the law they implement. Section 3506 of the TCCP required overtime to be paid by importers, shippers, or other persons served, which include airline companies, and not by all taxpayers through national funds (Carbonilla v. Board of Airline Representatives). (BOCEA v. Biazon, G.R. No. 205836, July 12, 2022)
alac.application: (1) Organizing work into three 8-hour shifts to provide 24-hour service and limit overtime is a measure to control work within the Bureau. It falls within the Executive's control over its personnel and is a valid and reasonable exercise of ordinance-making power. (2) Section 3506 placed the cost of overtime on the persons served, including airlines. A memorandum exempting airlines and charging overtime to the national government at government rates contradicts that law. In issuing it, the officials went beyond the law and committed grave abuse of discretion.
alac.conclusion: The shifting schedule is valid, but the prohibition on charging overtime to airlines is invalid.

bar_questions.q: Suppose the directive prohibiting Customs personnel from collecting overtime pay from airlines, and providing that the Bureau of Customs will pay all overtime work at service fees fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance, was issued only in March 2018. Would your ruling on its validity be the same?

alac.answer: No. A directive issued in March 2018 would be valid, because by then the governing law itself provided that the Bureau pays for overtime work.
alac.legal_basis: Section 3506 of the TCCP was repealed by RA No. 10863 (Customs Modernization and Tariff Act), effective June 16, 2016. Section 1508 of RA No. 10863 provides that Customs personnel assigned to overtime work "shall be paid for such services by the Bureau, according to service fees fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance." The Court held that this shift in policy was within Congress's discretion and legalized the policy of charging overtime to the Bureau starting June 16, 2016. (BOCEA v. Biazon, G.R. No. 205836, July 12, 2022)
alac.application: The 2013 directive was invalid because it contradicted Section 3506, which was then in force. A March 2018 directive would be measured against Section 1508 of RA No. 10863, which makes the Bureau, not the persons served, pay for overtime. It also requires the service fees to be fixed by the Commissioner and approved by the Secretary of Finance. A directive implementing exactly that scheme conforms to the law.
alac.conclusion: The 2018 directive would be valid because it conforms to Section 1508 of RA No. 10863.

bar_questions.q: A Customs employees' union filed directly with the Supreme Court a petition for certiorari and prohibition under Rule 65, assailing customs memoranda on overtime work, without first asking the Commissioner of Customs or the Secretary of Finance to reconsider them. The OSG argues that (i) certiorari does not lie against quasi-legislative acts, and (ii) the union violated the hierarchy of courts and failed to exhaust administrative remedies. (a) Rule on each argument. (b) If the Court reaches the merits and finds the memoranda partly invalid, may it also determine and order payment of the overtime differentials allegedly due the employees?

alac.answer: (a) The first argument is wrong, but the second is correct as a general rule. Certiorari lies against quasi-legislative acts under the Court's expanded jurisdiction, but the union should have filed with the CA after exhausting administrative remedies. The Supreme Court may still relax these rules in exceptional cases. (b) No. Monetary claims require the presentation of evidence and must be raised in the proper administrative or judicial proceeding.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article VIII, Section 1, paragraph 2 of the Constitution, the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction covers grave abuse of discretion by any branch or instrumentality of the government, so certiorari and prohibition may be used to assail quasi-legislative issuances. Even then, the petition must be filed with the lowest court of concurrent jurisdiction (the CA), and administrative remedies must first be exhausted, whether the act is quasi-judicial, quasi-legislative, or regulatory; failure to exhaust affects ripeness. The Court may set these rules aside where, as with the overtime pay of Customs employees, the issue has been the subject of long debate and repeated litigation. The resulting monetary prejudice is evidentiary and is for the trial courts, since the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts. (BOCEA v. Biazon, G.R. No. 205836, July 12, 2022)
alac.application: (a)(i) The memoranda are quasi-legislative, but the union alleges grave abuse of discretion by executive officials, which falls within the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction. (a)(ii) The union skipped the administrative route: reconsideration by the Commissioner, appeal to the Secretary of Finance, then the Office of the President. After that, judicial review would go to the CA under Rule 43 and then to the Supreme Court under Rule 45. Filing directly with the Supreme Court also violated the hierarchy of courts. The petition is dismissible, unless the Court, as it did in BOCEA, relaxes the rules because the issue has long been debated and litigated. (b) Determining whether employees received less than private-enterprise rates, and by how much, requires evidence. The Supreme Court will not make that determination in a certiorari petition; the claim must be pursued in the proper proceeding.
alac.conclusion: Certiorari is an available remedy, but the direct filing is generally improper absent exceptional reasons, and the overtime differentials cannot be adjudicated in the certiorari case.

notes: The petition also invoked Article VI, Sections 1 and 29(1) of the Constitution, labor laws, and due process. The main opinion resolved the case on the ordinance-making power and Section 3506 of the TCCP and did not separately rule on those other grounds. The caption names the Commissioner as "Rozzano Rufino B. Biazon", while the fallo refers to "Rufino B. Biazon". The effectivity date of RA No. 10863 (June 16, 2016) is as stated in the decision.
